notes: A deliberately strong counterpart to parking-lot-weak. It exists so the calibration test has an upper anchor as well as a lower one: a rubric that scores everything low is as broken as one that scores everything high. Note the structural properties it is built to have: 16 methods spread across 8 classes with a maximum of 3 on any one, so the D4 god-object check does NOT fire and the section 7.2.5 cap must not be applied to it.

assumptions: Multiple floors, each with a fixed number of slots configured at construction; the slot count does not change at runtime.

Slot size is fixed per slot and a vehicle occupies exactly one slot. Assuming fixed slot sizes; if sizes were dynamic, allocation would need to become a separate collaborator rather than living on Floor.
Payment is out of scope. We model the amount owed and mark a ticket as settled, but no gateway, no refunds and no currency handling.
Deliberately not modelled: reservations, season passes, and more than one lot. Nothing in the class list below refers to them.
Clarifying question: is pricing charged per started hour or per completed hour? The answer changes whether PricingPolicy needs the entry timestamp or only a duration.

classes.name: ParkingLot
classes.responsibility: owns the set of floors and answers where a vehicle can park

classes.name: Floor
classes.responsibility: holds its own slots and knows which of them are free

classes.name: Slot
classes.responsibility: represents one physical space and whether it is occupied

classes.name: Vehicle
classes.responsibility: identifies one vehicle and the slot size it requires

classes.name: Ticket
classes.responsibility: records entry time and the slot held, and is the unit pricing is calculated against

classes.name: PricingPolicy
classes.responsibility: interface: turns a closed ticket into an amount owed

classes.name: HourlyPricingPolicy
classes.responsibility: prices a closed ticket by started hours at a flat hourly rate

classes.name: WeekendPricingPolicy
classes.responsibility: prices a closed ticket at the weekend rate

relationships.note: ParkingLot owns its Floors; a Floor does not know the lot it sits in
Floor owns its Slots and is the only thing that hands one out
an occupied Slot points at the Vehicle in it; the Vehicle does not point back
Ticket records the Slot it was issued against by id, not by reference
pricing depends on the ticket, not the reverse, so pricing changes never reach the parking flow

tradeOffs: PricingPolicy is an interface because the requirements already name hourly and weekend rates. Two implementations exist today, so the abstraction is paid for rather than speculative.
No PaymentGateway interface: one processor is in scope and a second is not on the roadmap. The seam is Ticket.close(), and I would extract the interface when a second processor arrives, not before.

If electric-vehicle charging slots were required, I would add a ChargingSlot subtype of Slot and a ChargingRate implementation of PricingPolicy. Floor.firstFreeSlot would have to change because it must match on a capability and not only a size. Ticket, ParkingLot and the two existing pricing policies stay untouched.

The requirement my design handles badly is per-floor pricing. PricingPolicy is handed a Ticket that carries a slot id and no floor, so pricing would have to look the slot up. I would restructure by putting a small SlotDescriptor value object on the Ticket instead of a bare id.
